answer:
**A training budget can buy more parameters, more tokens, or a balance of both.** Under the illustrative relations D≈20N and C≈6ND, substituting gives C≈120N squared. Therefore N≈sqrt(C/120), and D is about twenty times that value. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)

If the budget quadruples within this fitted regime, both the preferred parameter count and token count approximately double. Increasing only model size while leaving data too limited can undertrain the larger model.

**The coefficient is empirical and the objective matters.** Data quality, architecture, repetition, and optimization change the tradeoff. A training-compute optimum does not include the cost of serving the model millions or billions of times.

A smaller model trained for longer may cost more to train than the training-only optimum but less over its lifetime because every inference is cheaper. Compare total training plus serving compute under quality and latency requirements. “Overtrained” relative to one budget definition can be economically sensible under another. State the workload and scaling regime before treating the 20-to-1 rule as a design law.

**Technical details and references.**

Under the illustrative Chinchilla rule $D\approx20N$ and training estimate $C\approx6ND$, substitution gives [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)

$$N\approx\sqrt{C/120},\qquad D\approx20\sqrt{C/120}.$$

Thus both parameter count and token count scale roughly as the square root of the training budget within that fitted regime. The coefficient is empirical, not a universal constant across architectures/data quality.

Serving many requests changes the objective: a smaller model trained on more data can cost more during training but less across billions of inference tokens. Optimize training plus lifetime serving cost subject to quality/latency, and account for data reuse/quality. “Overtrained” relative to a training-only optimum can be rational for a deployment-heavy workload.
